abstract: The British Standards Institution has just issued a revised and enlarged edition of B.S. 204, entitled Glossary of Terms Used in Telecommunication. This has been prepared in collaboration with the Post Office and several other organisations con nected with telegraph, telephone and radio industry and practice. It deals with the subject, of Section 9 (Telegraphs and Telephones) and Section 10 (Radio-com munication and Television) of the 1936 edition of B.S. 205 (Glossary of Terms used in Electrical Engineering) which were also published separately as B.S. 204, and of the supplement (C.F. 4420) to B.S. 205 (Radio Direction-finding). There is also a short newsection on fire alarms.

articleTitle: Some experiments on the automatic correction of power-factor to a predetermined value
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Mr. Teague lays some emphasis on the use by the author of a power-factor meter element for a balanced three-phase load. Most engineers are aware of the existence of elements comprising pressure and current coils designed to operate on unbalanced load. A big advantage of the apparatus under discussion over certain existing regulators for power-factor correction is that the apparatus can be used for unbalanced load by the simple substitution of the corresponding element. The author shares the opinion expressed by other engineers that the apparatus is capable of commercial development. With the extremely rapid corrective action of the device there is no need for the anti-hunting device referred to by the contributor. In view of the original line of approach to the problem of the automatic correction of power-factor, the question of infringement of existing patents does not arise.

abstract: A revised and considerably enlarged edition ofB.S. 308 has now been published. The recommendations for standard practice planning, numbering and referencing of series of drawings. Recommended scales, types of line, methods of projection, lettering, dimensioning and sectioning are set down, followed by standard methods of indicating machining symbols, surface finish, screw threads, bolts, nuts, rivets and welds. Notes on structural steelwork, a list of abbreviations for drawings and directions for the preparation of graphs complete the numbered clauses, which are followed by appendices dealing with the reproduction of drawings and the selection, preparation and storage of drawing paper, tracing paper and cloth, and sensitised materials. Other appendices contain references to British Standards formaterial specifications, general engineering standards and the use of symbols on drawings. The revised edition which is illustrated with 40 figures and diagrams and.four folded plates, supersedes B.S. 308-1927.

abstract: It is sometimes advocated, in the case of intermittent duty cycles, that the limiting factor is the equivalent heating over the period of the cycle. Thus, in the case of the example of the rotor circuit in which the current is 520 amps, for a period of 116 seconds, followed by an interval of one hour, equivalent heating would be produced by a sustained current of 91-5 amps. This would require, in air, a cable size of approximately 0-04 square inch compared to the size of 0-1 square inch as determined by the method advocated by the author.

articleTitle: Overhead power lines in south africa—the case for rationalisation
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: One would have thought that the paper would have evoked more discussion than it has. One feels, however, that while standardisation in detail will show a saving standardisation of design will not give the best results in all cases as it may not allow for local peculiarities. Our cost structure is so high that anything tending to increase power costs should be examined very closely, and no regulations having the effect of increasing capital costs should be advocated unless accurate statistical information justifies them; such statistical information should apply only to transmission lines, and should not include accidents due to all aerial lines as most accidents on overhead lines are probably due to the practice of taking service leads through corrugated-iron roofs.
